title: Expiring allocations: memory pages with a built-in death date
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Every allocation carries a TTL set by the programmer or inferred by the runtime (caches, session state, speculative buffers); the OS and memory controller reclaim expired pages without any free() call and stop refreshing those rows the moment they expire.
why: Cloud heaps carry 20-40% stale cache/session data nobody frees; TTL reclamation cuts resident footprint ~20-30% and drops refresh energy on dead rows (fact 3).

title: Client-carried KV cache: the user's device holds the server's memory
idea: Po: the user remembers the conversation, not the server. Between turns the server quantizes, entropy-codes, encrypts and MACs a session's KV cache and ships it to the user's phone/laptop/browser storage; the next request uploads it back, so the server holds zero KV for idle sessions.
why: Idle chat/agent sessions dominate KV residency; parking KV on billions of client devices cuts server DRAM/HBM for KV 5-20x, practical for contexts up to ~32k tokens on modern links.

title: Weight carousel: weights exist only in transit around an accelerator ring
idea: Po: the weights have no home. Model layers circulate continuously around an optical ring of accelerators; each node holds only a two-layer sliding window and applies it to its resident batch as the layer passes (data stays, weights move), so the cluster keeps one in-flight copy instead of one replica per data-parallel group.
why: Data-parallel inference replicates weights N times; the carousel cuts per-node weight memory roughly 20-60x for 80-layer models, trading DRAM for optical link bandwidth (fact 5).

title: Planet-once pages: content-addressed dedup inside the CXL memory switch
idea: Po: every byte exists only once on Earth. The rack's CXL switch hashes each 4 KB page written to pooled memory and maps identical pages (OS images, container layers, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) to one physical copy with copy-on-write, across all hosts rather than inside one hypervisor as KSM does.
why: Cross-host duplication in VM/container fleets is 15-40%; switch-level dedup recovers most of it with no per-host CPU scanning.

title: Predictive line coding: memory stores only what it could not guess
idea: Po: memory that lies, then gets corrected. A tiny predictor in the memory controller guesses each 64 B line from address neighbors and a per-page learned context (strides, pointer bases, float exponents); DRAM stores only the residual, which is near-zero for most lines and packed into variable-size slots, like inter-frame video coding for RAM.
why: 2-4x effective capacity on heaps and tensors where generic LZ gets ~1.5x; attacks cost per bit with no new cell.

title: Token-ID memory: keep the words, regenerate the KV on demand
idea: Po: the program remembers nothing. Long-context sessions keep only token IDs (2 B/token) plus full K/V for a few anchor layers; when attention needs the others, their K/V are recomputed from the anchors in one batched pass on otherwise-idle compute.
why: KV is ~100-300 KB/token for large models; tokens plus 10-20% anchor layers cut KV memory 5-10x, buying memory with cheap FLOPs.

title: Stranded-memory exchange: hourly auction of idle DRAM across tenants
idea: Po: your memory belongs to your neighbor. Cloud hosts expose DRAM left stranded when cores sell out first (typically 25-50%) into a CXL pool, and an exchange auctions it hourly to tenants' elastic caches under preemption contracts with posted prices.
why: Turns stranded capacity into supply; recovering half the stranded share raises usable fleet memory ~15-25% with zero new wafers.

title: Mask-ROM foundation models: freeze the weights in vias
idea: Po: RAM is read-only. Frozen, widely deployed model weights are fabricated as via-programmed multi-level mask ROM (only one or two masks change per model) on cheap mature-node wafers stacked under the accelerator; DRAM holds only activations and KV.
why: Weights are 50-90% of inference memory; ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and ~1-2 custom masks, cutting weight cost/bit several-fold and freeing DRAM for KV.

title: Nearest-neighbor KV residuals: store only how this prompt differs
idea: Po: every conversation is a rerun of another one. Incoming context is matched by embedding search to the closest cached context; its KV is stored as a low-bit quantized residual against that reference KV, extending prefix caching to near-duplicate, non-prefix content (templated documents, RAG chunks, code files).
why: Near-duplicate context is common in enterprise RAG/code workloads; residual coding could cut KV memory 3-8x beyond exact prefix sharing.

title: Fading KV: tokens lose bits as attention ignores them
idea: Po: memory that shrinks when you look away. Each KV entry carries an attention-usage counter and steps down 16 to 8 to 4 to 2 bits, then merges into a pooled summary vector, as its cumulative attention mass decays, mimicking human memory consolidation.
why: Most long-context tokens get negligible attention; graded decay gives 4-8x KV reduction with smoother quality loss than hard eviction.

title: Hash joins without hash tables: in-bank PIM probe units
idea: Po: the CPU lives inside the RAM. Compare-and-gather units beside each DRAM bank scan the build-side relation in place and stream out only matching tuple IDs, so analytical joins and group-bys never materialize multi-GB hash tables in main memory.
why: Intermediate hash tables can be 1-3x input size in analytics; in-bank probing removes them and cuts data-movement energy (facts 5, 8).

title: Half-size pointers: base-relative 32-bit addressing in the ISA
idea: Po: addresses cost nothing. An ISA extension adds region-base registers and load/store forms taking 32-bit (or 24-bit) offsets with hardware base addition, so C/C++/Rust programs and runtimes use compressed pointers everywhere, not only in JVM compressed oops.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, object heaps) is 30-50% pointers; halving them cuts footprint 15-25% and raises cache density.

title: Replay paging: record once, then run forever with oracle prefetch
idea: Po: memory arrives from the future. Recurring batch jobs (ETL, training epochs, nightly simulations) record their exact page-access trace on the first run; later runs replay it as a deterministic prefetch/evict schedule from SSD or CXL-flash, so DRAM holds only the lookahead window.
why: Repetitive jobs can run with 20-30% of peak working set in DRAM at near-zero stall, freeing capacity for interactive work.

title: Gang-swapped tenants: time-share whole memory images like CPU cores
idea: Po: only one program exists at a time. Low-duty-cycle VMs, notebooks and agents are gang-scheduled: each entire memory image is snapshotted to CXL-flash and restored in tens of milliseconds at 50+ GB/s when its slot comes, so host DRAM is sized for the active set, not all tenants.
why: Dev boxes, notebooks and agents idle >90% of the time; time-multiplexing their DRAM cuts provisioned memory 3-5x for those fleets.

title: Rumor memory: erasure-coded replicas instead of triple copies
idea: Po: data exists only as rumors spread among neighbors. In-memory databases and caches replace 3x replication with Reed-Solomon (e.g., 8+3) striping across nodes' DRAM and rebuild lost shards over RDMA on failure.
why: Cuts DRAM spent on fault tolerance from 200% overhead to ~37%, freeing about half of total memory in replicated stores.

title: Byte-rent compiler: auto-narrow every field to its observed range
idea: Po: programs pay rent for every byte per second. A profile-guided compiler pass records production value ranges and cardinalities, then recompiles structs with the narrowest integer widths, enums as bitfields and packed booleans, with guarded widening on overflow.
why: Typical business objects store 8-16-bit values in 64-bit fields; auto-narrowing cuts object footprint 30-50%.

title: Lifetime-predicted arenas: allocate objects by when they will die
idea: Po: garbage never exists. A learned model predicts each allocation's lifetime from its call-stack signature and places objects with similar death times in the same huge-page arena, which is released whole, so fragmentation holes never form.
why: Fragmentation and huge-page bloat waste 10-30% of server heaps; lifetime grouping recovers most of it.

title: Fuzzy structures: compiler swaps exact maps for sketches when allowed
idea: Po: memory is approximate by default. Developers annotate tolerances (e.g., count within 1%), and the compiler/runtime substitutes count-min sketches, HyperLogLog, quotient or Bloom filters for exact hash maps and sets in telemetry, dedup and analytics code.
why: Replaces GB-scale exact counters with MB-scale sketches: 100-1000x memory reduction for those structures.

title: Forward-only training: learn without storing the forward pass
idea: Po: training forgets the forward pass. Gradients come from forward-mode derivatives (JVPs with random tangents, variance-reduced by local layer-wise losses), so no activations are kept for backprop and memory stays O(one layer) regardless of depth.
why: Activations are often >50% of training memory; removing them could cut training DRAM/HBM 2-5x if the convergence penalty is contained.

title: Hot-line consolidation: memory tiering at 64-byte granularity
idea: Po: the page is one byte. The memory/CXL controller tracks hotness per cache line and migrates hot lines out of mostly-cold pages into dense hot-line pages in DRAM through a line-remap table, leaving cold remainders in compressed or far memory.
why: Page-granular tiering keeps 4 KB resident for a few hot lines; line-level consolidation shrinks the DRAM tier 2-3x for sparse-access workloads (fact 8 overfetch).

title: Generated embeddings: replace terabyte tables with tiny hash-fed networks
idea: Po: the table is stored inside a brain. Recommender embedding tables are replaced by a multi-hash encoder feeding a small MLP that generates each ID's embedding on the fly, with only the hottest ~1% of IDs cached explicitly.
why: Embedding tables are TB-scale DRAM hogs in recommendation; generation cuts them 10-100x at modest compute cost.

title: Fractional-reserve memory: oversell DRAM with a lender of last resort
idea: Po: memory banks lend memory like money. Hypervisors sell 1.5x physical DRAM based on a model of peak co-occurrence across VMs, backed by a compressed-memory plus CXL-flash central-bank tier that absorbs runs, with priced insurance for tenants wanting guaranteed residency.
why: VM memory is reserved at peak but used at average (often 40-60%); controlled overcommit yields ~30-50% more sellable memory per DIMM.

title: Born-compressed tensors: math on codebook indices, never decompressed
idea: Po: data is born compressed and dies compressed. Weights and KV are stored as vector-quantized codebook indices, and the accelerator computes dot products from precomputed lookup tables of codeword-by-query partial products, never expanding values to FP16 in memory.
why: Keeps weights/KV at 2-3 bits per value in DRAM (5-8x smaller than FP16) and cuts data movement in proportion (fact 5).

title: Manassas-plus: compressing CXL expander for domestic mature-node DRAM
idea: Po: America only makes yesterday's DRAM, so make yesterday's DRAM hold twice as much. A CXL Type-3 expander pairs Micron Manassas (VA) mature-node DRAM with a GlobalFoundries Malta (NY) 12LP+ controller doing inline LZ-class and zero-line compression with variable-size line mapping, assembled on U.S. EMS lines.
why: 2-3x effective capacity lets domestic older-node DRAM match imported leading-edge DIMMs on cost per usable bit, raising U.S.-only supply with no new fab.

title: All-SRAM American inference box: zero DRAM, logic-fab memory only
idea: Po: memory made only of logic transistors. Intel 18A (AZ/OR) SRAM chiplets hybrid-bonded 8-high with Foveros Direct in Rio Rancho (NM) hold a 4-bit entropy-coded model whose attention/state-space hybrid design has fixed-size recurrent state, so KV never grows and no DRAM is needed.
why: Sidesteps the lack of leading-edge U.S. DRAM by using U.S. logic capacity that exists; fits inference in ~10-40 GB of SRAM and slashes data-movement energy (fact 5).

title: MRAM commit buffer: dirty pages leave DRAM the instant they are written
idea: Po: dirty pages are already safe. An Everspin (Chandler, AZ) STT-MRAM persistent write buffer on a domestic CXL card acknowledges database commits and redo records at byte granularity, so OLTP buffer pools no longer pin dirty pages or double-buffer log data while waiting for flush.
why: Write-heavy databases oversize buffer pools ~30-50% to absorb dirty pages and log buffers; persistent commit lets that DRAM shrink.

title: Weights as wires: models compiled into fixed logic on 18A
idea: Po: the weights are welded into the chip. A frozen model is synthesized into constant-coefficient multiplier/adder trees (weights folded into gates, shared partial products via canonical-signed-digit recoding) on Intel 18A or Samsung Taylor (TX) 2 nm and packaged in the U.S.; only KV and activations need DRAM.
why: Removes weight storage and weight fetch entirely: DRAM per inference node drops by the weight share (50-90%) and energy per token ~10x, using U.S. logic fabs instead of foreign DRAM.

title: Resistor weights from Minnesota: ReRAM compute tiles on SkyWater 130
idea: Po: the resistor is the weight. ReRAM integrated into SkyWater's Bloomington (MN) 130 nm flow stores edge and agent-model weights as multi-level conductances in crossbars that do matrix-vector products in place with on-chip ADCs, so weights never touch DRAM.
why: A DUV-only, trusted U.S. fab with no EUV runs small models DRAM-free, removing weight-fetch energy and DRAM footprint for edge fleets.

title: Rack memory commons: a domestic CXL switch pools all DRAM
idea: Po: servers own no memory. A CXL 3.x switch ASIC fabbed at GlobalFoundries Malta links 16-32 hosts to shared drawers of U.S.-made DRAM; hosts keep small local DIMMs and borrow the rest at ~250 ns, with the pool sized for the rack's aggregate peak, not the sum of per-host peaks.
why: Statistical multiplexing cuts provisioned DRAM 20-30% per rack, stretching scarce U.S.-made bits.

title: One-brain package: CPU and accelerator share memory, no staging copies
idea: Po: the CPU and the accelerator are the same animal. CPU and accelerator dies co-packaged with Foveros in New Mexico share one coherent pool of U.S.-made DRAM, eliminating duplicate pinned host buffers, dataloader staging copies and host-side mirrors of device tensors.
why: Discrete-accelerator hosts often carry 1-2x accelerator memory in host DRAM for staging; unification cuts host DRAM 30-50%.

title: Blurry numbers: error-bounded compression of live simulation state
idea: Po: numbers are blurry on purpose. DOE-lab error-bounded lossy compressors (SZ/ZFP class) run inline in the memory path of U.S.-built supercomputer nodes, keeping field data compressed under a user-set pointwise error bound and decompressing per tile on access.
why: Scientific floating-point fields compress 5-20x within physics-acceptable error, so domestic HPC fits larger problems in the same DRAM.

title: Negabytes: pay to free memory like utilities pay for negawatts
idea: Po: we pay people to un-buy memory. A federal program modeled on utility demand-side programs pays a verified $/GB-year for DRAM freed through software or architecture changes, measured by fleet telemetry; freed U.S.-made modules are bought back and redeployed to defense, research and domestic manufacturers.
why: Software efficiency is the cheapest domestic fab; a negabyte market could free 10-20% of installed U.S. DRAM within a few years at a fraction of fab capex.

title: Execute-in-place code tier: domestic NOR serves read-only program text
idea: Po: there is no NAND fab in America, so use the flash America still makes. Infineon Austin (TX) NOR flash on a CXL card is mapped as byte-addressable read-only memory, and the loader maps code segments, shared libraries and read-only data directly from it (execute-in-place) so they never occupy DRAM.
why: Code and read-only data are 10-25% of microservice footprints; XIP from domestic NOR (100 ns-class reads, CPU-cached) frees that DRAM with no NAND imports.

title: Zygote fleets: every microVM is a copy-on-write clone
idea: Po: every program is a clone of one ancestor. Serverless and microservice fleets on U.S.-built servers boot one golden, fully warmed microVM per runtime and fork every instance from it copy-on-write, Android-zygote style at VM scale, so warm pools share runtime, JIT code and heap prefixes.
why: Warm-pool memory is mostly identical runtime state; CoW forking cuts per-instance resident memory 3-10x, stretching scarce domestic DRAM.

title: Pointerless graphs: succinct structures for national-scale analytics
idea: Po: data structures without pointers. Graph, trie and index workloads (knowledge graphs, genomics, search) are rebuilt on succinct encodings (rank/select bitvectors, wavelet trees, Elias-Fano adjacency) and queried in compressed form on domestic CPUs.
why: Succinct encodings approach information-theoretic size, 5-10x smaller than pointer-based graphs, so national datasets fit the limited U.S.-made DRAM.

title: One cache only: merge the database buffer pool with page cache
idea: Po: there is only one cache in the machine. A kernel interface lets databases and storage engines adopt the OS page cache as their buffer pool, with app-controlled eviction hints and pinning, eliminating the second copy of every hot page on U.S.-made servers.
why: Double caching wastes up to 2x on hot data; unifying recovers 20-40% of DRAM in storage-heavy servers.

title: Live-set-sized heaps: hardware read barriers for pauseless compaction
idea: Po: the heap is exactly as big as the live data. A load-barrier ISA extension (colored-pointer check and forwarding in hardware) on a U.S.-designed core fabbed at Intel Arizona makes concurrent compacting GC nearly free, so managed heaps run at 1.1-1.2x live set instead of 2-3x headroom.
why: Java/Go/.NET heaps are routinely provisioned 2-3x live data to keep GC cheap; hardware barriers could cut managed-heap DRAM ~40%.

title: Split objects: hot fields stay, cold fields shrink and move out
idea: Po: every object is cut in half. A profile-guided compiler peels each struct into a hot part (fields touched on fast paths) and a cold part that is batch-compressed in a separate region and reached through a 4-byte handle only when rare paths need it.
why: Cold fields are often 50-70% of object bytes; peeling and compressing them cuts resident footprint 25-40% on domestic hardware.

title: Data never comes home: query predicates applied in the network path
idea: Po: the data never enters memory. Intel Agilex FPGAs (Intel 7, fabbed in Oregon/Arizona) sit in the NIC path and apply predicates, projections and decompression to incoming storage and network streams, so host DRAM buffers hold only matching rows and needed columns.
why: Scan-heavy analytics pull 10-100x more data into DRAM than queries use; near-data filtering shrinks buffer memory and bandwidth in proportion.

title: Pruned-to-customer MoE: deploy only the experts real traffic wakes
idea: Po: a customer only needs the experts they actually use. Each domestic deployment profiles a week of its own traffic, drops experts with negligible routing mass, patches the router with a small distilled fix-up for residual tokens, and serves the slimmed MoE on U.S.-made hardware.
why: Domain traffic typically activates a minority of experts; pruning 50-70% of them shrinks weight memory in proportion with small task-quality loss.

title: Sleep consolidation: agents distill yesterday's context into small adapters
idea: Po: yesterday's conversation becomes today's neurons. Long-lived agents compress their accumulated context nightly into a low-rank adapter (tens of MB) by self-distillation on U.S.-fabbed accelerators, discarding the GB-scale KV cache and keeping only a short summary window.
why: Persistent agent memory moves from O(context) KV (GBs) to O(1) adapters (MBs): 50-100x less memory for long-running agents.

title: Memory rationing by merit: domestic DRAM goes to efficient workloads
idea: Po: memory is rationed like wartime sugar. Under Defense Production Act priority authority, domestic DRAM output and federal cloud memory go first to workloads certified on a public bytes-per-unit-work benchmark (GB per 1k inferences, per query), with tiers reset yearly.
why: Turns scarce U.S.-made supply into an efficiency incentive: vendors cut footprint to get supply, compounding 10-30% savings across federal and defense computing.

title: Unikernel diet: specialized library-OS images for every service
idea: Po: the operating system is part of the app. Services built with a domestic hardened toolchain are linked into single-address-space unikernels holding only the OS components they call, dropping per-VM kernel, init, daemon and page-table overhead from ~150-300 MB to ~10-20 MB.
why: In dense microservice fleets guest-OS overhead is 20-40% of DRAM; unikernels reclaim most of it on U.S.-made servers.

title: Tattletale chip: domestic per-page access counters for exact tiering
idea: Po: memory that tattles on itself. A small GlobalFoundries Malta-fabbed companion chip on each CXL memory module counts activations per page (and per line in hot pages) from the command stream and publishes heatmaps, replacing the CPU's imprecise page-table scanning.
why: Exact hotness lets the fast DRAM tier be sized to the true hot set (often 20-40% of footprint) and doubles as row-hammer telemetry (fact 9).

title: Scarcity chargeback: bill teams the real price of gigabyte-hours
idea: Po: every line of code shows its memory price tag. Enterprises and agencies charge internal teams the current spot price of U.S.-made DRAM per GB-hour, and CI gates block merges that push a service past its byte budget without sign-off.
why: Makes memory cost visible where it is decided; chargeback programs typically cut consumption 15-30% within a year with no new hardware.

title: Three-life DIMMs: cascade U.S.-made modules from AI to edge
idea: Po: the same 42 mg of silicon is sold three times. U.S.-made modules are leased with take-back: first life in AI servers, then re-tested and re-binned (speed, ECC margin, row-hammer threshold) in U.S. facilities for web tiers, then remounted on CXL cards for cold-tier and edge use, stretching service life from ~5 to ~10-12 years.
why: Roughly halves new-DRAM demand per unit of deployed capacity over a decade and keeps scarce domestic bits in service.
